title_th: การพูดคุยประจำวัน
register: Casual-friendly (first names, contractions, short turns; workplace-neutral)

words_in_context: Not bad, thanks. And you? (/ən juː/)
It depends on the weather. (/ən ðə/)
a bit of a mad month (/ə bɪd əv ə/)
targets.why_it_matters_here: Small talk lives inside unstressed function words. If you say 'How HAVE YOU BEEN?' with every word full and equal, it lands like a job interview and the other person gives you a one-word answer and walks off. And in the other direction: if you cannot hear weak 'can' /kən/ against stressed 'can't' /kɑːnt/, you will agree to Friday drinks you already said you couldn't make, and then not turn up.
targets._note: taught and drilled, never metered - vendor gives no en-AU prosody data

words_in_context: Cold today, isn't it? (rise on the tag)
And you? (rise — hands the turn back)
Really cold. (fall — agreement, not a question)
Sorry, Dan's thing? (rise — I didn't catch that)
Good to see you! (warm fall — closing)
targets.why_it_matters_here: In small talk, intonation IS the meaning. A flat 'Nice.' after your colleague says they got married reads as bored or sarcastic, and people remember that. A flat 'And you.' closes the conversation instead of passing it back, so the chat dies in three seconds and you get labelled unfriendly at work — when you were only being careful with your English.

shadow_focus_lines.text: Yeah, me too. Good to see you!

chunk_drills.label: Open it (and hand it straight back)
examples: How's it going? — Not bad, thanks. And you?
How was your weekend? — Quiet, actually. How about you?
How've you been? — Busy! And you?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles greetings_and_goodbyes; adds present perfect in the fixed chunk "How've you been?" with the weak form /haʊv jə bɪn/ — learners say it as a chunk, not as grammar.

chunk_drills.label: The safe vague answer + one small detail
chunk_drills.pattern: "Not much. / Nothing special. / Just the usual." + "Maybe ___."
examples: Not much. Maybe the market on Sunday.
Just the usual. I might catch up with friends.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles days_and_times ('on Sunday', 'Saturday morning') and 'maybe / might' for unfixed plans.

chunk_drills.label: Weather + tag question (rising)
chunk_drills.pattern: "[Adjective] today, isn't it?" / "It's supposed to ___, isn't it?"
examples: It's supposed to rain Saturday, isn't it?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles weather_words; tag questions drilled purely for rising intonation, not for tag formation rules.

chunk_drills.label: Keep it going: one short follow-up question
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Short elliptical questions ('Where to?', 'How long for?') — full sentences not required at A2.

chunk_drills.label: React before you answer
chunk_drills.pattern: "Really? / Oh no. / That's awful. / Nice! / Fair enough." + your line
examples: Oh no. I hope it's better now.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Fixed reaction chunks; scored on intonation contour rather than on words.

chunk_drills.label: Ask again without panic
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles asking_for_clarification; rising intonation on the repeated word signals 'I missed that', not 'I disagree'.

chunk_drills.label: Close it politely
chunk_drills.pattern: "Anyway, I'd better ___." + "Good to see you! / Have a good one."
examples: Anyway, I'd better run. Good to see you!
Anyway, I'd better get back. Have a good one.
Right, I'd better go. See you Monday!
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: 'I'd better + verb' taught as one chunk with weak /aɪd/; recycles days_and_times in the goodbye.

listening_items.audio_text: Hey, how's it going? Haven't seen you in ages — how've you been?
listening_items.channel: face-to-face, office corridor, fast and friendly
listening_items.question: Is the speaker asking about right now, or about the last few weeks?
listening_items.answer: About the last few weeks — 'How've you been?' (they haven't seen you in a long time).
listening_items.distractor_focus: 'How've you been' compressed to /haʊv jə bɪn/ can be heard as 'How you been' or 'How are you' — learners must catch the weak 've'.

listening_items.audio_text: I can't make Friday, sorry — but I can do Saturday afternoon.
listening_items.question: Which day is the speaker free?
listening_items.answer: Saturday afternoon. They cannot do Friday.
listening_items.distractor_focus: Weak 'can' /kən/ versus stressed 'can't' /kɑːnt/ — mishearing this reverses the whole message.

listening_items.question: Is this a question or a statement?
listening_items.answer: A question — the voice rises at the end, so they want an answer.
listening_items.distractor_focus: Same words, falling contour ('You're coming on Friday.') would just be confirming a fact; intonation is the only clue.

listening_items.audio_text: It's his leaving drinks. Six o'clock, at the pub near the station — not the office one.
listening_items.question: What time, and which pub?
listening_items.answer: Six o'clock, at the pub near the station (not the one near the office).
listening_items.distractor_focus: Recycled numbers plus a correction tucked into the end of the turn — learners often stop listening after the time.

listening_items.question: Does the speaker sound genuinely pleased or unimpressed?
listening_items.answer: Unimpressed / not really interested — the flat, falling delivery makes 'lovely' sound insincere.
listening_items.distractor_focus: Trains learners to hear (and then avoid producing) flat contours on reaction words like 'lovely', 'nice', 'great'.

guided_roleplay.learner_role: You are at work on Monday morning. A friendly colleague you like — but don't know well — starts chatting while the kettle boils. Keep the conversation alive for about a minute, then leave politely.
flow: Step 1 — Answer the opener and hand it back: reply to 'How's it going?' in two or three words, then ask 'And you?'
Step 2 — Do the weather: agree with their comment, or start one yourself with a rising tag ('Cold today, isn't it?').
Step 3 — Weekend exchange: give a vague answer plus one small detail, then ask them the same question.
Step 4 — Keep it going: react ('Really? / Oh no. / Nice!') and ask ONE short follow-up question ('Where to?', 'How come?').
Step 5 — Repair: they mention a name, a place or a time you don't know. Say 'Sorry, ___?' and get it repeated.
Step 6 — Close it: 'Anyway, I'd better run. Good to see you!' — with warm falling intonation, not an abrupt stop.
sentence_frames: Good to see you! / Have a good one.

free_roleplay.ai_persona: Sam — a warm, chatty colleague in their thirties. Uses first names, contractions and very short turns. Never lectures, never corrects grammar mid-chat; if the learner stalls, Sam offers a friendly prompt ('Big weekend, or a quiet one?') and waits.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Sam stays on the predictable script: greeting → weather → weekend plans → warm goodbye. Short turns, one question at a time, generous pauses. Sam accepts vague answers ('Not much') and models the follow-up question the learner didn't ask.
b1_curveballs: Sam drops mild bad news — 'we moved house and it was a nightmare' or 'I've been off sick, actually' — and the learner must react appropriately and ask one follow-up before moving on.
Sam jumps topic with no warning: from the weather straight to 'Are you coming to Dan's thing on Friday?' The learner must ask 'Sorry, Dan's thing?' and get the details.
Sam invites the learner somewhere at an awkward time ('six o'clock Friday') and the learner must half-decline without killing the mood ('I'll try — six is a bit early for me').
Sam asks the learner a question back that needs more than a word: 'So what have you been up to?' — the learner must produce two or three linked sentences.
Sam uses fast weak forms and swallowed words ('Whaddya up to this weekend?', 'D'you wanna come?') and the learner must ask for a repeat instead of guessing.
Sam tries to end the chat first ('Right, I'd better run') and the learner must close warmly rather than keep talking.

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Answered the opener briefly and handed the turn back with 'And you?' / 'How about you?'
Covered at least two small-talk topics (e.g. weather and weekend), recycling days, times or weather words
Kept it going: reacted at least twice ('Really?', 'Oh no.', 'Nice!') and asked at least one follow-up question
Used a clarification move ('Sorry, ___?') instead of guessing or going silent when something was missed
Closed the conversation politely with a closing chunk ('Anyway, I'd better run. Good to see you!') rather than stopping dead
Stayed casual-friendly: contractions, short turns, no over-formal 'I am very fine, thank you very much'
Pronunciation: weak forms in 'And you?', 'How about you?', 'I'd better run' are reduced, and intonation rises on questions/tags and falls warmly on reactions and the goodbye
Stretch (B1): handled a curveball — mild bad news, a sudden topic jump, or an awkward invitation — with an appropriate reaction and kept the chat going for another turn or two

register_culture_note.en: Small talk is not information exchange — it is a two-minute friendliness ritual. Nobody wants a full report. 'Not bad, you?' is a complete, successful answer. The two rules that matter: keep your turns short, and always pass the ball back with a question. Use contractions and reductions ('How've you been?', 'And you?'); full careful forms sound like an interview. Safe topics almost everywhere: weather, weekend, traffic, food, the coffee. Risky in English-speaking workplaces: money, weight, age, relationship status, religion.

do_dont.avoid: "I am very fine, thank you, and how are you?" (full forms, every word stressed)
do_dont.prefer: "Not bad, thanks. And you?" — short, with weak 'and' and a rising 'you?'

do_dont.avoid: Answering 'How've you been?' with a two-minute account of your health, your family and your job
do_dont.prefer: One line plus a question: "Busy, actually. How about you?"

do_dont.avoid: Going silent when you miss a word, then smiling and nodding
do_dont.prefer: "Sorry, Dan's thing?" — repeating the word with a rise is friendly, not rude

do_dont.avoid: Flat, falling "Nice." or "Really." after someone's news (sounds bored or sarcastic)
do_dont.prefer: "Nice! Which beach?" — reaction with a rise or a warm fall, plus a follow-up

do_dont.avoid: "You look tired. How old are you? How much do you earn?"
do_dont.prefer: "Busy week? / How was your weekend? / Any plans for the long weekend?"

do_dont.avoid: Walking away mid-topic with no closing line
do_dont.prefer: "Anyway, I'd better run. Good to see you!"

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: Two habits carry over from Thai and cause real trouble. First, questions that are ordinary care in Thai — how old are you, how much do you earn, have you put on weight, are you married yet — read as intrusive in most English-speaking workplaces; keep to weather, weekend and food until you know someone well. Second, in Thai it is often polite to let a senior colleague lead and to answer briefly without asking back; in English, not returning the question ('And you?') is read as coldness or disinterest, not respect. Your job in small talk is to keep the ball in the air for a minute — even with your boss. Also note: 'How are you?' from a passing colleague is a greeting, not a real enquiry, so a short cheerful answer is exactly right; and this is one of the few situations where mild complaining about the weather counts as being friendly.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can answer 'How's it going?' briefly and hand the question back with 'And you?'
I can make and answer a comment about the weather using a tag question.
I can say what I did or might do at the weekend in one or two short sentences.
I can end a short chat politely with 'Anyway, I'd better run. Good to see you!'
I can keep a conversation going for a minute or more by reacting and asking short follow-up questions.
I can respond appropriately when someone shares mild bad news, and then move the chat on.
I can handle a sudden topic change or an unclear invitation by asking for clarification and getting the details.
My weak forms ('And you?', 'How've you been?', 'I'd better run') are reduced, and my intonation rises on questions and falls warmly on reactions and goodbyes.

unlocks: Topic Juggler badge — three topics in one conversation without a dead stop
Ball Back badge — returned the question five times in a row
Repair Kit badge — used 'Sorry, ___?' successfully instead of guessing
Smooth Exit badge — closed three chats with a natural closing chunk
sound_meters: weak_forms — reduction meter on 'And you?', 'How about you?', 'How've you been?', 'I'd better run'
intonation — rise/fall meter: rising tags and questions vs warm falling reactions and goodbyes
Streak meter: consecutive turns where reaction + follow-up question both landed
